Before you start the task, you must find out how dangerous the turbulence, buffet, or the
in−flight maneuver was. You do this by an analysis of the related flight data.

(FDR) with a portable analysis unit (PAU). The downloaded data is then plotted on a
graph and analyzed. As an alternative, a detailed report from the flight crew should be
obtained. Based upon the graph analysis or flight crew report, a visual inspection of the
aircraft may be required.

When the wiring and/or connectors are examined, a failure can be caused by a bent

(19)
Standard handling and safety precautions must be obeyed when work is done with
electrical components and circuits. Refer to AMM TASK 24−00−00−910−801,
Electrical/Electronic Safety Precautions. Schematics or wiring diagrams must be
examined to find the applicable circuit breakers to open before you disconnect the
related component(s). For safety awareness, applicable high−voltage warning
placards are put in many areas of the aircraft.
G.
Voltage and Continuity Measurements
(1)
Most voltage and continuity checks can be done with standard volt/ohm meters.
Voltage checks are usually done at connector pins, which are accessible in the
aircraft. These are specified when possible.
(2)
Voltage checks at most relays are done after the relay is removed. They are usually
attached by two or three captive screws. The isolation procedures refer to the
appropriate wiring diagram or the AMM removal/installation procedure in the first
block of any isolation path where a circuit check is necessary. The WM or AMM
reference will not be shown again until the corrective action block shows "Replace
the relay (WM _ _ _ _ _ _)".
(3)
In a fault isolation procedure, when a relay, switch or component replacement is
called out and there is no AMM removal/installation related task available, the WM
chapter and system reference will be supplied. The WM reference should be used
to determine the correct circuit breaker to be pulled before removing and installing
the related relay, switch or component.
(4)
Standard procedures for relay sockets, switches, components and wiring
maintenance are shown in Chapter 20 of the WM.
(5)
When you do a fault isolation procedure that requires the removal or installation of
an electrostatic − sensitive discharge device, make sure that you closely follow the
procedures found in the AMM, Chapter 24, TASK 24−00−00−910−802, Electrostatic
Discharge Safety Precautions.
(6)
When the wiring and/or connectors are examined, a failure can be caused by a bent
pin, unlocked pin, corrosion, and open circuit or a shorted circuit. Once the
inspection of the connectors and pins is done, examine for wiring abrasion and
shorted or open connections. Examine grounding studs and pins carefully for signs
of corrosion or poor connection between the stud and airframe ground.
(7)
Standard handling and safety precautions must be obeyed when work is done with
electrical components and circuits. Schematics or wiring diagrams must be
examined to find the applicable circuit breakers to open before you disconnect the
component(s). For safety awareness, refer to AMM TASK 24−00−00−910−801,
Electrical/Electronic Safety Precautions. Applicable high−voltage warning placards
are put in many areas of the aircraft.

36−21−07−000−805). If time permits, test the thermal switches until you find

components described in this procedure.

TASK 36−21−10−000−801) to confirm the fault (fault indication moves to the

09-10-00-584-802.title:
1.
General
A.
The maintenance procedures that follow are for the movement of aircraft on the ground
by maintenance persons with a towing vehicle.
B.
TASK 09−10−00−584−801 gives the procedure for towing an aircraft with the steering
torque links disconnected. This is used to tow or push the aircraft to a different location
with a towing vehicle.
C.
TASK 09−10−00−584−802 gives the procedure for the push back of an aircraft with the
steering torque links disconnected. This is used to move the aircraft away from the
terminal gate before a flight, with the flight crew members on board.
D.
TASK 09−10−00−584−804 and gives the procedure for the push back of an aircraft with
the steering torque links connected. This is used to move the aircraft away from the
terminal gate before a flight, with the flight crew members on the aircraft. This procedure
is also used to move the aircraft back with the ground towing crew only. The procedure
for the ground towing crew is given. When the flight crew is on the aircraft, the steps of
the procedure that are done in the flight compartment can be ignored.
E.
TASK 09−10−00−584−805 gives the procedure for the movement of an aircraft with a
towbarless vehicle. Towbarless towing is permitted for push back and maintenance
towing. It is not permitted for dispatch towing.
F.
Turn angle limits must not be more than 70 degrees right and left from the center.
Markings that you can see in all lighting conditions must be attached to the nose gear
strut at +/− 70 degrees from the center line. The towing operator must be able to clearly
see at all times when he approaches the nose gear turn limits.
G.
It is preferable to keep the torque links connected during push back maneuvers. If you
do disconnect the torque links where steering angles above +/− 70 degrees are
necessary, refer to the push back procedure with torque links disconnected (TASK
09−10−00−584−802).
H.
If one or more engines or the horizontal stabilizer are removed, the center of gravity (C
of G) of the aircraft will move forward. In this configuration, you can tow the aircraft
without special precautions. If equipment is removed from the forward fuselage, it is
possible that the aircraft C of G will move too far aft to tow the aircraft. The C of G must
not be aft of FS540.50 for safe movement of the aircraft. The tail of the aircraft can tilt
down to the ground in the worst condition. If necessary, refer to the Weight and Balance
Manual, section 01−80−10, to calculate the position of the aircraft C of G.
I.
For more safety when the aircraft C of G is near the aft limit, you can install a ballast
assembly at the nose jacking point (Ref. TASK 07−11−01−582−801).

(1)

weather or accidents.

and Ground tiedowns) (refer to Figure 1) to do the following:
NOTE:
The aircraft must be on firm level ground, preferably tarmac or concrete,
with the nose pointing into the prevailing wind. Also follow the precautions
listed for parking the aircraft in an open area.
NOTE:
To reduce any pitching tendency, it is recommended that the aircraft be
fully fueled and the center of gravity moved as far forward as possible.
(a)
Anchor the aircraft (refer to Figure 2) in position relative to the jacking points
and the hoist ring locations where the mooring kit components are installed.
Mooring adapter plates are installed at each aircraft jacking point to moor the
wings and nose. Each adapter plate is attached to the aircraft with a jacking
pad. There are two tiedown rings on each adapter plate.

Mooring tiedown rings (refer to Figure 2) are installed on the bottom of the rear
fuselage to moor the aircraft tail. The attachment points for the tiedown rings
are installed in the bottom fuselage skin left and right of the fuselage center at
FS755.00.

28-11-00-620-801.title:
TASK 28−11−00−620−801
Biocide Treatment of the Fuel Tanks
1.
General
A.
The maintenance procedure that follows is for the biocide treatment of the fuel tanks
(written as the "treatment" in this procedure. This procedure is applicable only if no
biocide fuel additive is already present in the fuel system. The procedure is necessary to
sterilize (shock treatment) and keep (regular maintenance) the fuel system clean from
the biological contamination as a result of fungi and the bacteria in the fuel. These fungi
grow into long strings and form large mats or globules.
NOTE:
To most effectively control biological contamination, remove all the water and
debris from the fuel system before, and regularly after, the biocide treatment.
The water in the fuel tanks will cause the formation of solids.
NOTE:
The maintenance procedure for the shock treatment and the regular
maintenance is identical (unless otherwise indicated). The shock treatment is
necessary when the microbial growth is first found in the fuel tanks. The
regular maintenance is then applied as a preventive measure, for new fuel
tanks or when the aircraft is scheduled to operate in very hot climatic
conditions.
NOTE:
After a shock treatment, a fuel sample is taken to check for water, biological
growth, and corrosion particle contamination. Dying microorganisms may
release particles of dirt and corrosion that have been caught in the mats. Slime
will come off the fuel tank wall and structure as it is killed. An inspection of the
fuel system and components is necessary if slime, biological growth, or
corrosion particle contaminants are found in the fuel.
NOTE:
For Biobor JF, the concentrations of biocide fuel additive are given as parts per
million (ppm) by weight. The maximum allowable concentration of the biocide
fuel additive is 270 ppm.
NOTE:
For Kathon FP 1.5, the concentrations of biocide fuel additive are given in ppm
by volume.
NOTE:
For Biobor JF, to avoid the formation of solids, do not let the concentration of
biocide fuel additive be more than 1000 ppm at any time.
NOTE:
For Biobor JF, to be most effective, let the biocide fuel additive stay in the fuel
tanks for a period of 36 to 72 hours.
NOTE:
You may do the biocide treatment only in the main tanks, only if the center
tank never contained fuel.
NOTE:
Fuel containing biocide fuel additive can be used for operation if the
concentration is not higher than 270 ppm for Biobor JF or 100 ppm for Kathon
FP 1.5 as specified in the Flight Crew Operating Manual (FCOM).

12-20-27-640-806.title:
1
If a jam because of low temperature operation (water or too much grease
in the drive system) is suspected, do the steps that follows:
a
Disconnect the flexible drive shaft from each side of each applicable
actuator as necessary (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−801), the
drive shaft No. 2 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−802), the drive
shaft No. 3 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−803), the drive shaft No.
4 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−804), the drive shaft No. 5 (Ref.
AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−805).
b
Examine the couplings for signs of water or corrosion. If water is found
in the flexible drive shafts, do the pressure test of the flexible drive
shaft (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−00−780−801). If the flexible drive shaft
passes the pressure test, clean the flexible drive shaft (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−53−10−220−802). Replace the flexible drive shafts that have
corrosion.
c
With the core disconnected at both ends, turn the core by hand to feel
for binding conditions, then remove the core.
d
Examine the core for too much grease (there should be a thin layer
only), damage to the core windings or corrosion.
e
Replace the flexible drive shafts that have damaged core windings or
corrosion.
f
If there is too much grease but no other damage, re−lubricate the core
with the correct quantity and type of grease (Ref. AMM TASK
12−20−27−640−806).
g
Install the core.  Make sure that the core moves in and out of the
casing freely and can be turned by hand.  Replace flexible drive shafts
that are difficult to turn by hand.
h
Remove the 4 actuators from the wing and do the low temperature
torque test on each one (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−00−750−801).
Replace the actuators that fail the low temperature torque test.
2
If a jam because of mechanical drive system faults is suspected, do the
steps that follow:
a
Examine the flap actuators for visible signs of actuator damage or
leakage from the front housing of the actuator.  Replace actuators
where grease leakage is sufficient to form a run down the face of the
actuator front housing (gearbox).
b
Move the flap trailing edge up and down in line with each actuator as
the ballnut and forward end of the ball screw are observed.  If there is
visible fore/aft movement of the ballnut on the ballscrew, or of the
ballscrew in the actuator front housing, replace the actuator.  If you are
not sure about the amount of fore and aft movement and want to
measure the actuator’s endplay, refer to the Component Maintenance
Manual for the actuator.
c
Operate the flaps for 5 cycles, finishing with the flaps at 45 degrees.
During flap movement, listen to each actuator and also the PDU for
abnormal grinding, howling or other noises.  Replace a PDU or actuator
that makes abnormal sounds.

12-11-28-750-804.title:
constant with the data from the fuel probes to calculate the fuel quantity in each fuel
tank. Total fuel quantity and fuel−used data are also calculated by the fuel system
computer.
B.
Fuel quantity information is supplied to the refuel/defuel control panel and to the flight
compartment on the engine indication and crew alerting system (EICAS) display. The
fuel system computer also uses this data to calculate fuel balance. If there is a fuel
imbalance of more than 200 pounds (90 kg), the fuel system computer will operate the
transfer system (28−13−00) to move fuel from one main tank to the other.
C.
Fuel quantity information is also used to control fuel transfer from the center tank to the
main tanks. If the fuel level in either of the main tanks is less than 93 percent full, the fuel
system computer will operate the fuel transfer system. The fuel transfer system then
moves fuel from the center tank to the applicable main tank. Fuel transfer will continue
until the main tank is 97 percent full.
D.
During automatic refuel operations, the fuel system computer uses fuel quantity
information to control the pressure refuel/defuel system (28−25−00). Fuel quantity
information from the fuel system computer is supplied to the refuel/defuel control panel
for all pressure refuel/defuel operations.
E.
If there is a failure of the fuel−quantity gauging system, the fuel level can be measured
when the aircraft is on the ground. The operator uses the fuel magnetic level−indicators
to measure the level of the fuel in each fuel tank. The operator then examines the aircraft
attitude indicators to measure the aircraft attitude. With this data, the operator examines
a reference table found in the AMM (Ref. TASK 12−11−28−750−804) to calculate the
fuel level in each tank.

1.
Reason for the Job

21-51-13-140-801.title:
– In which area of the aircraft was the oil smell found?
B.
General information.
(1)
If odor in the flight compartment or in the cabin is caused by oil, or other
contamination that goes into the core engine, clean the compressor (Ref.
TASK 72−00−00−100−801).
(2)
Clean or replace the coalescer bags of the air conditioning system after any
maintenance task that removed the flight compartment or cabin odor (Ref. TASK
21−51−13−140−801).
(3)
You can remove a fan blade retaining−pin for borescope access of the No. 1
bearing retainer plate and the compressor front−frame cavity to help isolate the
source of the oil leakage.
(4)
Remove the oil or oil residue before you do the last engine tests to make sure that
the problem does not occur again.
(5)
Refer to Steps C. thru E., and the fault isolation logic chart in Figure 101 and isolate
the flight compartment or cabin odor. Refer also to Table 101 for more instructions
related to the fault isolation charts.
C.
Isolate the fault to the aircraft systems as follows:
(1)
Use the aircraft bleed air controls, found on the BLEED AIR panel, to isolate the
auxiliary power unit (APU) and the left or right engine.
(2)
Replace the APU (Ref. TASK 49−10−00−000−801) or clean the dirty coalescer
socks of the air conditioning system (Ref. TASK 21−51−13−140−801) as
necessary.
D.
Isolate the fault to internal oil leakage as follows:
(1)
Leakage of the No. 1 carbon seal is shown by oil leakage from the A−sump drain
(at the overboard drain) and/or by oil wetting around the fan vanes at the inner
diameter ends and around the fan static seal and front frame 6 o’clock drain hole.
No. 1 carbon seal leakage is also shown by oil wetting on the forward/aft faces of
the No. 1 bearing support plate. You can see the No. 1 bearing support plate with a
borescope put through a fan−blade pin hole with the blade and pin removed. For a
No. 1 carbon seal to cause an oil smell in the flight compartment or cabin, there is
oil wetting in the core inlet area (between the fan vanes and the forward stages of
the compressor).

If a fault condition was reported and there are no related SECU fail log fault codes,
suspect a "soft fault" condition. Do the fault isolation flow chart− Spoiler
System"Soft Faults" given in Paragraph 9.
(6)
A SECU module shutdown can be caused by a short circuit in a PCU bypass valve
solenoid or wiring. If you interchange or replace a SECU before you find and correct
this condition, you can cause damage to the replacement SECU. Do
resistance/insulation tests of the PCU bypass valve solenoid (Ref. AMM TASK
27−62−01−760−801) before you install a different SECU in place of the one that
was removed.
**ON A/C 7240−7990, 8000−8400 and ON A/C 7003−7067, 7069−7217 Post SB601R−27−088
CAUTION:
DO NOT CLOSE AN OPEN CIRCUIT BREAKER ON THE SPOILER
CIRCUIT−BREAKER PANELS UNLESS A
RESISTANCE/INSULATION TEST OF THE PCU BYPASS−VALVE
SOLENOID IS DONE OR THE PCU IS REPLACED.  YOU CAN
CAUSE DAMAGE TO THE SECU.
CAUTION:
DO NOT INSTALL A REPLACEMENT SECU IF THERE IS A
POSSIBILITY OF A SHORT CIRCUIT IN THE BYPASS VALVE
SOLENOID OF A PCU.  IF A REPLACEMENT SECU IS
INSTALLED BEFORE THE PCU’S ARE TESTED FOR SHORT
CIRCUITS, THE PCU WITH THE SHORT CIRCUIT CAN CAUSE
DAMAGE TO THE REPLACEMENT SECU.

attached to the seat tracks, push forward on the
pilot’s control column (against the restraint of the
rigging pin) and push forward on the restraint rods as
the seat track clamps are tightened to hold the control
column as rigidly as possible.
(d) Attach a digital protractor to the aft side of the
copilot’s control column.
(e) Use the force gauge to apply a 3.5−4.5 lb (16−20 N)
forward load to the top of the copilot’s control
column.  As the load is held, set the digital protractor
to zero.
(f)
Apply the same load to the copilot’s control column in
the aft direction and measure the backlash.
(g) The maximum backlash permitted between the
control columns is 0.38 degrees (equivalent to 0.200
inch (5.0 mm) fore/aft travel measured at the copilot’s
wheel and the seat tracks.

27-00-10-830-801.title:
– Bit 30=1 and bit 31=1 − LRU Failed.
Refer to Table 101 to troubleshoot from the MDC Label 350 indications. For other
fault conditions, refer to the Troubleshooting Notes in the subsequent paragraph
3.
Troubleshooting Notes
A.
If a fault is detected in the CFMS through the LRU STATUS page, the LRU
DIAGNOSTIC DATA page or the ECU LED remains on, before removing any
components, do the zero rigging of the crew force measuring system (Ref. AMM  TASK
27−00−10−830−801). If the  ECU LED goes out and any messages clear from the LRU
STATUS / LRU  DIAGNOSTIC DATA pages, no more action is required.

27-31-02-000-801.title:
PILOT’S ELEVATOR CONTROL SENSOR FAILURE
Replace the pilot’s elevator force sensor (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−31−02−000−801)
and do the zero rigging of the crew force measuring system (Ref. AMM  TASK
27−00−10−830−801).  If the fault occurs again, check the wiring between the ECU
at the connector (P14WR−A) and the sensor (J15WR) (Ref WM 31−31−00).
Repair the wiring as necessary. If the wiring is okay, remove the ECU (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−00−10−000−802) and replace it with a known good one, and do the zero
rigging of the crew force measuring system (Ref. AMM  TASK
27−00−10−830−801).

General
A.

27-13-10-000-801.title:
ROLL DISCONNECT SWITCH FAILURE
Each SECU gets a ground through separate contacts in the roll
disconnect switch when the roll disconnect handle is operated.
Do the steps that follow:
A.
Remove the SECU with the failure indication (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−61−05−000−801).
B.
Operate the roll disconnect handle to the unlock
position (fully up).
C.
Measure for a ground at pin 11E of connector 1P1CN−A
or 2P1CN−A in the applicable SECU tray. If there is no
ground, do an installation check of the roll disconnect
switch (Ref. AMM TASK 27−13−10−400−801).
D.
If the switch is adjusted correctly, there is a probable
failure of the switch or its related wiring. Replace the
switch (Ref. AMM TASK 27−13−10−000−801) or repair
the wiring as necessary.
E.
If the switch operates correctly, replace the SECU with
the failure indication .
F.
Make sure that any SECU that was removed, and was
not replaced with a different one, is installed in its
original location.

27-11-06-000-802.title:
PILOT’S AILERON CONTROL SENSOR FAILURE
Replace the pilot’s aileron force sensor (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−11−06−000−802)
and do the zero rigging of the crew force measuring system (Ref. AMM  TASK
27−00−10−830−801).  If the fault occurs again, check the wiring between the ECU
at the connector (P14WR−A) and the sensor (J21WR) (Ref WM 31−31−00).
Repair the wiring as necessary. If the wiring is okay, replace the ECU (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−00−10−000−802), and do the zero rigging of the crew force measuring
system (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−00−10−830−801).
NOTE:
In the case of a sensor rupture or sensor disconnect, the control wheel
torque will be transmitted to the aileron control circuit through stops
machined in the aileron input/output quadrant. In this case, the maximum
angular deflection will be ± 4.0 degrees. This will be detected by
excessive free play at the control wheel.

27-11-15-720-801.title:
(1)
Remove the applicable roll priority switch (Ref.
AMM TASK 27−61−20−000−801).
(2)
Test the operation of the switch directly from
the switch terminals. Replace the switch if
necessary.
(3)
If the switch operates normally, test the wiring
between the SECU and the switch (Ref. WM
27−60−00). Repair the wiring as necessary.
C.
If the roll priority switch operated correctly when tested
from the SECU tray, a possible cause of the fault is a
defective latching relay for the bungee breakout switch
in the tension regulator or the related wiring. Do the
steps that follow:
(1)
Get access to the tension regulator for the
applicable side and install a rigging pin in the
tension regulator (Ref. AMM TASK
27−11−15−720−801).
(2)
As the control wheel is turned sufficiently to
operate the breakout switch in the tension
regulator, (approximately 1/4 of a turn of the
handwheel), measure for a ground at pin 4H
(pilot) or 5H (copilot) of the applicable SECU
tray connector 1P1CN or 2P1CN.
(3)
When you get a ground, move the control
wheel back to neutral, and make sure that the
ground continues. Pull circuit breaker CB 4−A4
(SECS 1 PWR 3) for SEC 1, or CB4−A5 (SECS
2 PWR 3) for SECU 2 and make sure that the
ground is removed when the circuit breaker is
pulled.
(4)
If you don’t get a ground or the ground does
not continue until you pull the circuit breaker,
there is a defect in the latching relay K1CN
(left) or K2CN (right) in junction box 10, or the
related wiring. Replace the relay or repair the
wiring as necessary.
D.
If no faults were found in the roll priority circuits external
to the SECU, replace the SECU.
E.
Make sure that any SECU and/or ADC that was
removed, and was not replaced with a different one, is
installed in its original location.

27-35-05-000-801.title:
AOA FAILURE
This is a failure of the left or right angle−of−attack transducer. If the SPC
is able to identify which transducer is defective (such as a complete loss
of signal or a disagreement between the two signals within the same
transducer) the transducer is identified by SDI bits 9 and 10. If bit 9=1/bit
10=0, the failure is of the left AOA transducer; if bit 9=0/bit 10=1, the
failure is of the right AOA transducer. To avoid unnecessary AOA
transducer removals, do the functional test of the AOA transducer (Ref.
AMM TASK 27−35−05−720−801) to verify the MDC results.
Refer to figure 102. Replace the AOA transducer that is not in tolerance
as specified of the AOA Test Result  Data Sheet (Ref. AMM TASK
27−35−05−000−801).
If the SDI bits do not identify whether the failure is left or right, the SPC
has detected a mismatch between the left and right dual AOA signals but
is unable to determine which signal pair is valid and which is faulty. An
internal mechanical defect such as a bent input shaft or gear wear that
results in valid but incorrect dual resolver signals from one of the
transducers could cause this condition. To identify a defective
transducer, do the functional test of the AOA transducer (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−35−05−720−801).
Replace the AOA transducer that is not in tolerance as specified of the
AOA Test Result Data Sheet (Ref. AMM TASK 27−35−05−000−801).

27-35-15-000-801.title:
STICK PUSHER FAILURE
Bit 20=1 when there is a failure detected by internal detection circuits in
the stick pusher actuator. A failure results in a ground signal to both
channels of the SPC at the same time.
There is also a parallel potential ground path with a zener diode that
provides overvoltage protection for the failure detection circuit. A short
circuit failure of that diode could be seen by the SPC as a ground and
therefore a fail signal. Also a short to ground of the wiring itself could be
seen by the SPC as a fail signal.
Because the ground signal is supplied to both SPC channels at the
same time, the fault should be shown for both channels. If bit 20=1 for
one channel only, there is a probable wiring short between the SPC
channel and junction box JB−11, or an internal SPC fault.
Do the steps that follow when bit 20=1:
A.
Replace the stick pusher actuator (Ref. AMM TASK
27−35−15−000−801).
B.
Reset the SPC memory and run the pre−flight test. If the fault is
cleared, return to service. If the fault occurs again, replace the
SPC with a known serviceable unit and run the pre−flight test
again. If the fault occurs again, there is a probable short to ground
that is causing the SPC to latch a false failure. Do the steps that
follow:
(1) Remove the SPC (Ref. AMM TASK 27−35−01−000−801).
(2) Disconnect the electrical connector P8CG at the stick pusher
unit.
(3) At the SPC mounting tray, test for a ground at pins 4C and
4H of connector PC7G−A. There should not be a ground with
connector P8CG disconnected.
(4) If a ground is found at pins 4C and 4H with connector P8CG
disconnected, there is a probable failure of the zener diode
CR5CG in junction box JB−11 (Ref. WM 27−35−00) or a
wiring short. Test for wiring shorts, and if none are found,
replace JB−11
(Ref. AMM TASK 24−01−11−000−801).

27-35-25-000-801.title:
PRIMARY MACH FAILURE
Bit 13=1 is a loss of mach number input to the stall protection computer,
or the mach number input is considered invalid by the SPC, which
compares the input with the 3 other primary/secondary inputs.
This fault will only be latched when the aircraft is in flight. Therefore,
once the fault is cleared by an SPC memory reset, you cannot make the
fault occur again unless the aircraft is put weight−off−wheels and
airspeed is brought to more than 65 kt with the air data test set. If the
necessary equipment or time to simulate an airborne condition is not
available to confirm the fault, proceed based on the fault indication that
was originally set in flight.
If bit 9=1/bit 10=0, the fault is in the left mach transducer; if bit 9=0/bit
10=1, the fault is in the right mach transducer.
Replace the applicable left or right mach transducer (Ref. AMM TASK
27−35−25−000−801). If the fault occurs again, replace the opposite
mach transducer.

(3)
Points to note about mach number input "failure" and "disagree" indications on
Label 350:
(a)
The SPC monitors the two primary (mach transducers) and secondary (ADC
ARINC 429 mach number input) mach number inputs continuously to detect
faults. Faults are detected on a "voting" basis. If one input disagrees with the
other three by more than a preset limit, an applicable "primary mach" or
"secondary mach" failure bit is set on MDC SPS Label 350.
(b)
If there is a variation in an input value that is not sufficient to be considered a
failure, but was outside of the normal values, a "mach transducer disagree" bit
is set. This is an indication that there was a variance in signal, but the variance
was too small for the SPC to decide which of the four signals was at fault.
(4)
There can be other failure conditions where the information in SPS Label 350 may
be insufficient for troubleshooting. These conditions and the necessary actions are
given as follows:
(a)
During Pre−flight Test, the stick pusher fails to operate, and bit 20 (stick
pusher fail) and/or 21 (pusher output failure) of SPS Label 350 is not set:
1
There is a probable mechanical failure of the capstan or drive pulley that
connects to the elevator quadrant.
2
Examine the cable circuit of the stick pusher system, the quadrant and
other mechanical components for signs of damage or jam conditions.
Replace cables or other components as necessary.
3
If no signs of mechanical damage are found, replace the stick pusher
capstan (Ref. AMM TASK 27−35−20−000−801).
(b)
Pushing the STALL switch/light fails to start the Pre−flight Test and there are
no faults shown on MDC label 350:
1
To start the pre−flight test, a voltage is applied to the self test inputs of the
two SPC channels. The STALL switch/lights are wired in parallel, so that
either switch can start the pre−flight test. Power to both switches is routed
through relay K1CG in junction box JB−10, which is energized closed via
the PSEU when the aircraft is weight−on−wheels.
2
Therefore, if the pre−flight test cannot be started from one side, but starts
normally from the other side, the probable cause of the fault is an open
contacts failure of the applicable STALL switch/light or a failure of the
related wiring. Replace the applicable STALL switch/light (Ref. AMM TASK
27−35−35−000−801) or repair the wiring.
3
If the pre−flight test cannot be started from either STALL switch/light, the
aircraft is weight−on−wheels (no PSS FAULT MESSAGES), and there are
no SPC channel failures, there is a probable fault in relay K1CG in junction
box JB−10 that controls the power supply to the two STALL switch/lights.
Replace JB−10 (Ref. AMM TASK 24−01−10−000−801).
(c)
During Pre−flight Test, the STALL light fails to come on and bit 24 (visual
warning output failure) of SPS Label 350 is not set:
1
Operate the LAMP TEST switch on the miscellaneous test panel to confirm
the serviceability of the light bulbs and circuitry for the STALL light.

27-52-05-000-801.title:
– PDU motor mechanical fault or dragging brake (fault code 9).
NOTE:
This fault is internal to the PDU or FECU and not from an external
jam because the high current condition was detected on one PDU
motor and not the other.
(d)
PROCEDURE:
1
If this message is associated with Fault Log codes EE  8  FF (Motor
Current > Stall), there was a sudden and rapid increase in current to 26
amps.  The probable cause is a short to ground in the left PDU motor, its
wiring, or channel 1 the FECU.  Do the steps that follows:
a
Remove the FECU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−51−05−000−801).
b
Disconnect the electrical connector from the indicated PDU motor.
c
Test the 3−phase wiring between the PDU motor connector and the
FECU mounting tray for open circuits and shorts to ground (refer to
Part 2, Paragraph 6).  Repair the wiring as necessary.  If there are no
wiring faults, continue.
d
Do a megohmmeter check of the 3−phase wiring for the PDU motor at
the motor receptacle (refer to Part 2, Paragraph 6).
e
If a fault is found in the PDU, replace the PDU as follows:
1) Remove the PDU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−52−01−000−801).
2) Install a new (Ref. AMM TASK 27−52−01−400−801).
f
If no wiring faults or PDU faults are found, replace the FECU as
follows:
1) Remove the FECU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−51−05−000−801).
2) Install a new FECU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−51−05−400−801).
2
If this message is associated with fault codes EE  9  FF (Motor Current =
Stall), there was a gradual increase in current to the stall value.  The
probable cause is an internal motor or gearbox fault or a dragging brake.
Do the steps that follows:
a
Do FECU Test 4 (left Motor/Brake test) or 5 (right Motor/Brake test) as
applicable.  If the test fails, replace the PDU as follows:
1) Remove the PDU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−52−01−000−801).
2) Install a new PDU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−52−01−400−801). If the
test passes continue.
b
Remove the FECU (Ref. AMM TASK 27−52−05−000−801) and
disconnect the electrical connector for the applicable PDU motor.

27-53-00-750-802.title:
– Flap panel fouling on adjacent structure.
(d)
PROCEDURE:
1
Examine the flap panels for signs of fouling on adjacent structure during
flap movement.
2
Examine the flexible drive shafts for signs of a kinked or crushed drive
shaft casing that could pinch the drive shaft core.  Replace the applicable
flexible drive shaft section as follows:
a
Remove drive shaft section (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−801), the
drive shaft No. 2 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−802), the drive
shaft No. 3 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−803), the drive shaft No.
4(Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−804), the drive shaft No. 5(Ref.
AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−805) for the drive shaft No. 5.
b
Install a new drive shaft No. 1 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−400−801),
the drive shaft No. 2(Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−400−802), the drive
shaft No. 3(Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−400−803), the drive shaft No.
4, (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−400−804), the drive shaft No. 5 (Ref.
AMM TASK 27−53−10−400−805).
3
Do a torque check of the flap drive system (Ref. AMM TASK
27−53−00−750−802).
4
If the torque check passes, operate the flap drive system manually through
its full range of travel (Ref. AMM TASK 27−54−00−866−803). Turn the
draft shaft and feel for an increase in torque (binding) in the drive system.
5
If you can feel a binding condition at a given position, keep the drive
system at that position and do the AMM torque check procedure again to
measure the torque increase caused by the binding condition and to isolate
its location. Replace the unserviceable flap actuator as follows:
a
Remove the inboard flap actuator (Ref. AMM
TASK27−53−01−000−801) and the outboard (Ref. AMM TASK
27−53−01−000−801) for the outboard flap actuators.
b
Install a new inboard flap actuator (Ref. AMM
TASK27−53−01−400−801) and the outboard flap actuator (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−53−01−400−801).

27-61-20-000-801.title:
(1)
Remove the applicable roll priority switch (Ref.
AMM TASK 27−61−20−000−801).
(2)
Test the operation of the switch directly from
the switch terminals. Replace the switch if
necessary.
(3)
If the switch operates normally, test the wiring
between the SECU and the switch (Ref. WM
27−60−00). Repair the wiring as necessary.
C.
If the roll priority switch operated correctly when tested
from the SECU tray, a possible cause of the fault is a
defective latching relay for the bungee breakout switch
in the tension regulator or the related wiring. Do the
steps that follow:
(1)
Get access to the tension regulator for the
applicable side and install a rigging pin in the
tension regulator (Ref. AMM TASK
27−11−15−720−801).
(2)
As the control wheel is turned sufficiently to
operate the breakout switch in the tension
regulator, (approximately 1/4 of a turn of the
handwheel), measure for a ground at pin 4H
(pilot) or 5H (copilot) of the applicable SECU
tray connector 1P1CN or 2P1CN.
(3)
When you get a ground, move the control
wheel back to neutral, and make sure that the
ground continues. Pull circuit breaker CB 4−A4
(SECS 1 PWR 3) for SEC 1, or CB4−A5 (SECS
2 PWR 3) for SECU 2 and make sure that the
ground is removed when the circuit breaker is
pulled.
(4)
If you don’t get a ground or the ground does
not continue until you pull the circuit breaker,
there is a defect in the latching relay K1CN
(left) or K2CN (right) in junction box 10, or the
related wiring. Replace the relay or repair the
wiring as necessary.
D.
If no faults were found in the roll priority circuits external
to the SECU, replace the SECU.
E.
Make sure that any SECU and/or ADC that was
removed, and was not replaced with a different one, is
installed in its original location.

Operational Test of the APU Fuel Control Unit

49-31-01-991-802.title:
E.
Do a check for fuel leaks from the APU fuel−feed line, as follows:
(1)
Visually inspect APU fuel inlet hose at the FCU connector for traces of fuel leakage.
There must be no leakage.
(2)
Visually inspect the APU fuel−feed tube at the center tank connector for traces of
fuel leakage. There must be no leakage.
(3)
When a leak is found, do the steps that follow:
(a)
Open, safety, and tag the circuit breakers referred to in para. 1H.
(b)
Disconnect the APU fuel inlet hose to the FCU inlet port, when fuel leaks at
this connection (Ref. TASK 49−31−01−991−802). Or, disconnect the APU fuel
feed tube at the center tank connector, when fuel leaks at this connection.
(c)
Inspect both applicable connector parts for foreign objects or damage.
(d)
Reconnect the APU fuel inlet hose to the FCU inlet port, when applicable (Ref.
TASK 49−31−01−400−801). Or, reconnect the APU fuel−feed tube at the
center tank connector. Tighten the connector to 210 to 420 inch pounds (23.71
to 47.42 Nm).
(e)
Remove the tags and close the circuit breakers referred to in para. 3B.
(f)
Do again the operational test of the FCU (Ref. TASK 49−31−01−710−801).
(4)
Connect the APU fuel−feed shroud (9) to the APU fuel−feed connector and tighten
the clamp (8).

28-21-04-000-801.title:
A.
If the right check valve was replaced, do a test as follows:
(1)
Start the left engine (Ref. TASK 71−00−00−868−806).
(2)
On the FUEL synoptic display, make sure that the left and right electric boost
pumps are not shown in green.
NOTE:
Left and right boost pumps set to off.
(3)
Wait for up to two minutes. Make sure that the caution message R LO FUEL
PRESS is shown in amber on the EICAS primary page.
NOTE:
When the R LO FUEL PRESS message is not shown, the left
fuel−feed−line−check valve has possibly failed in the open position.
(4)
When necessary, do an engine dry motor cycle (Ref. TASK 71−00−00−868−811) to
find if the left fuel−feed−line−check valve is serviceable.
NOTE:
When the R LO FUEL PRESS caution does not show, the left
fuel−feed−line−check valve must be replaced.
(5)
Do a shut down of the left engine (Ref. TASK 71−00−00−868−807).
(6)
When necessary, replace the left fuel−feed−line−check valve (Ref. TASK
28−21−04−000−801 and TASK 28−21−04−400−801) and do this test again.

terminal stud on the switch.

based on the results given below:

edges on the ground, and goes out when the hot air supply is removed and the
leading edge cools down. Go to paragraph C. (3).

paragraph C. (4).

to paragraph C. (5).

71-00-00-868-804.title:
1.
Definition of the Condition
Refer to Figure 101
A.
Definition of a Hot Start
NOTE:
For the engine overtemperature limits, refer to AMM TASK
71−00−00−868−804, Engine Operating Limits.
(1)
During an engine start, there is a very fast increase of the interturbine temperature
(ITT), possibly related to an engine stall.
Possible causes for a Hot Start are:
(a)
The throttle adjustment.
(b)
Problems with the Variable Geometry (VG) system.
(c)
A bleed−air removal rate that is too high.
(d)
An internal engine damage.
(e)
A defective fuel control unit (e.g. too much fuel is metered to the engine during
a start).
CAUTION:
IF THE ITT REACHES 800 °C AND IS RISING RAPIDLY DURING AN
ATTEMPTED START, THEN MOVE THE THROTTLE LEVER TO THE
SHUTOFF POSITION AND CONTINUE TO OPERATE THE STARTER
TO MAINTAIN ITT WITHIN THE STARTING TEMPERATURE LIMITS.  IF
YOU DO NOT, YOU WILL CAUSE DAMAGE TO THE EQUIPMENT AND
COULD CAUSE A FIRE.
B.
If it is a short time since the engine was shut down, dry motor the engine (Ref.
AMM TASK 71−00−00−868−811) until the ITT is less than 120° C before you try to start
the engine again.
C.
If you think there was an ITT indication shift, do the troubleshooting of the thermocouple
harness and the white electrical cable (FIM 77−10−00, Figure 104). If not, continue with
the troubleshooting as perFigure 101.
2.
Troubleshooting
A.
Before you start the troubleshooting, find out the information that follows:
(1)
What was the maximum temperature during the start? Was the temperature higher
than the permitted limits?
(2)
Did the HOT icon come on in the EICAS display during the start? The HOT icon
comes on if the ITT is more than 500° C and increases at a rate of more than 200°
C per second.

TASK 32−47−01−000−802
Removal of the Brake Application Pressure Transducer
1.
General
A.
The maintenance procedures that follow are for the removal and installation of the brake
application pressure transducers (written as the ‘pressure transducers’ in this
procedure).  The digital flight data recorder uses the pressure transducers to monitor the
application of brake pressure downstream of the brake system volumetric fuses.  The
are four pressure transducers − two for the outboard brakes (hydraulic system No. 2)
and two for the inboard brakes (hydraulic system No. 3).
B.
The pressure transducers are installed on mounting plates in the MLG bay,  near the
volumetric fuses.  The pressure transducers for the left MLG are installed at FS 530 and
LBL 23 approximately.  The pressure transducers for the right MLG are installed at
FS 530 and RBL 23 approximately.

If the N/W STRG switch was cycled to clear an intermittent NWS system
failure, it is possible that no Maintenance Display Code will be displayed on the
seven−segment maintenance display of the ECU.
To determine what the intermittent fault was, go to the EICAS MAINTENANCE
MENU page and do a check on the LRU FAULT HISTORY page for LRU
DIAGNOSTIC DATA words that were stored in the MDC NVM for that flight leg
(Refer to Table 101 and FIM 45−45−00).
NOTE:
This page is a record of only those LRU faults that were diagnosed
while the aircraft was in the air or within 30 seconds after landing.
If you are not able to diagnose the fault do a check on the LRU FAULT
HISTORY page for LRU DIAGNOSTIC DATA words on the LRU DIAGNOSTIC
DATA page (Refer to Table 101 and FIM 45−45−00). These data words are
displayed on (or removed from) the LRU FAULT HISTORY page in real time.
NOTE:
If you are not able to diagnose the fault using the MDC NVM, do an
interrogation of the ECU NVM (Ref. AMM
TASK 32−51−10−700−801).
(c)
When you have made a record of all of the data, cycle the N/W STRG switch
to try to clear all of the faults.
(d)
If the fault was cleared when the power reset was done, do an operational test
of the ECU (Ref. AMM TASK 32−51−10−710−801) to try to make the fault
occur again.

32-51-10-400-801.title:
M.
If the NWS system ECU was replaced with a new one (Ref. TASK 32−51−10−400−801),
do the steps that follow to prepare the ECU for the operational test and to correctly
update the calibration values in the new ECU:
NOTE:
If the NWS system ECU was not replaced with a new one, go to the next step.
NOTE:
This step will make sure that the new ECU is updated with the correct RVDT
calibration values to prevent RVDT nuisance faults. If a new ECU is not
updated with the current calibration values of the NWS system RVDTs, it is
possible that an incorrect STEERING INOP indication will be seen on the
primary page of the engine indication and crew alerting system (EICAS)
together with the Maintenance Display Code "E" on the seven−segment
maintenance display of the ECU when you do the next step.
(1)
Put the N/W STRG switch on the pilot’s side panel in the ARMED position.
NOTE:
For this step only, ignore the amber STEERING INOP indication if it is
shown on the primary page of the EICAS.
(2)
On the front of the NWS ECU set the OPR/RIG switch to the RIG position. Make
sure that the Maintenance Display Code "A" is seen on the seven−segment
maintenance display of the ECU. When the Maintenance Display Code "A" is
shown, the ECU is in RIGGING MODE. In this mode, the solenoid selector valve
(SSV) is disabled to allow steering system components to be rigged.
(3)
Set the OPR/RIG switch on the front of the NWS ECU to the OPR position. Make
sure that the Maintenance Display Code "C" is seen on the seven−segment
maintenance display of the ECU. When the Maintenance Display Code "C" is
shown, the ECU has completed a RIGGING sequence satisfactorily and the
calibration values of the NWS system RVDTs are correct.
NOTE:
All of the steering system RVDTs must be in the electrical−null (straight
ahead) position for this indication to be shown. The ECU is now in
OPERATING MODE. In this mode, the SSV is still disabled. The ECU will
not return to GROUND MODE until electrical power is cycled with the
N/W STRG switch.
(4)
Cycle the N/W STRG switch on the pilot’s side panel to the OFF position and then
to the ARMED position. Make sure that the Maintenance Display Code "C" changes
to a full size "0".
NOTE:
When the full size Maintenance Display Code "0" is shown, the ECU is in
GROUND MODE. In this mode, the ECU will respond to steering
command inputs and will provide control signals to the electrohydraulic
servo valve and the SSV. The ECU is in GROUND MODE when:

Alternate Compensating Swing of the Remote Compensation Unit
CAUTION:
AN AHRS SYSTEM ALIGNED BY THE PROCEDURE GIVEN IN THIS TASK
CANNOT BE USED AS A HEADING REFERENCE TO ALIGN THE SECOND
AHRS, UNTIL A COMPLETE COMPENSATING SWING IS DONE (REF. TASK
34−21−07−820−801).  IF THE AHRS SYSTEM IS USED AS A HEADING
REFERENCE TO ALIGN THE SECOND AHRS, INCORRECT INDICATIONS CAN
OCCUR.
1.
General
A.
The maintenance procedure that follows is for the alternate compensating swing of the
remote compensation unit. This procedure can be used to align the attitude and heading
reference system (AHRS) after the failure of a single system only. In this procedure, the
fully serviceable AHRS is used as the heading reference. This procedure is applicable to
remote compensation units 1 and 2. Data for remote compensation unit 2 is given in
parentheses.

49-81-01-220-802.title:
AMTOSS 49−81−01−220−801
1.
Reason for the Job
Refer to MRB 49−81−00−01
2.
Job Set−Up
A.
Open the aft equipment compartment door (311BB).
B.
Remove the APU access panel (311BZ).
3.
Procedure
Refer to Figure 1.
A.
Do a detailed inspection of the APU exhaust duct assembly as
follows:
(1) Examine the blanket that covers the APU exhaust duct for
security of attachment.
(2) Examine the blanket for signs of exhaust gas leakage and
damage.
(3) Examine the drain fitting for evidence of cracks or
damage.
(4) Examine the bellows assembly for damage.
(5) Examine the exhaust nozzle assembly inside the APU
enclosure, for damage, wear, and cracks.
(6) Examine the exhaust deflector for damage.
(7) Examine the heat shield for security of attachment.
(8) Examine the heat shield and the fuselage skin for damage
and cracks.
(9) From outside the aircraft, examine the inside of the duct
for cracks and damage.
NOTE:
If damage is found, refer to Damage Limits of the
Exhaust Duct Assembly, TASK
49−81−01−220−802.
4.
Close Out
A.
Remove all tools, equipment, and unwanted materials from the
work area.
B.
Install the APU access panel (311BZ).
C.
Close the aft equipment compartment door (311BB).

51-21-11-620-802.title:
1.
General
A.
The maintenance practices that follow supply instructions to prevent corrosion on bare
metal surfaces. The steps to apply corrosion prevention treatment are as follows:
(1)
Apply the necessary chemical and/or mechanical treatments to the surfaces of all
the metallic aircraft parts that have corrosion damage.
(2)
Apply chemical surface treatments and primer. If necessary, apply treatment to the
surfaces that are open to galvanic corrosion.
(3)
Where necessary, apply a paint finish.
NOTE:
If a paint finish is necessary, apply it as quickly as possible after you
apply the surface treatment and primer.
B.
Corrosion prevention treatments use the procedures that follow:
(1)
Alodine Solution Treatment (TASK 51−21−11−380−801).
Manually−applied Alodine solutions (conversion coatings) are used to chemically
treat isolated areas where protective surface coatings are removed. You can also
use this procedure to apply a conversion coating on small locally−made repair
parts. Two types of manually−applied coatings, known as Type I and Type II are
used. They are specified as follows:
(a)
Type 1 is a transparent, colorless coating with low electrical resistivity that you
get with Alodine 1000 (or equivalent) solution. Type I coating is used when the
color you get from the Type II solution is unwanted or electrical bonding is
necessary. Type I coatings are not as good as Type II coatings for the
prevention of corrosion.
(b)
Type ll is a coating with a yellow or gold color that you get with Alodine 1200S
(or equivalent) solution. Use Type II coatings in all areas where you do not
have to use Type I coatings.
(2)
Fastener Installation Treatment (TASK 51−21−11−620−802).
C.
To apply other corrosion prevention treatments, refer to the SRM 51−21−11 for the
procedures that follow:

52-11-13-820-802.title:
Refer to Figure 402.
WARNING:
USE A SUFFICIENT NUMBER OF PERSONS TO HELP OPEN OR CLOSE THE
PASSENGER DOOR WHEN THE COUNTERBALANCE SPRINGS ARE
DISCONNECTED. THE DOOR WEIGHS APPROXIMATELY 280 POUNDS (127
KG). IF YOU DO NOT OPEN OR CLOSE IT CAREFULLY. IT CAN CAUSE
INJURY TO PERSONS AND DAMAGE TO EQUIPMENT.
CAUTION:
WHILE THE GAS SPRING CABLES ARE DISCONNECTED, MAKE SURE THAT
THE SWIVEL LEVERS POINT INBOARD.  IF THE DOOR IS CLOSED WITH THE
LEVERS IN THE DOWN POSITION, THEY WILL CAUSE DAMAGE TO THE
DOOR.
G.
Connect the aft counterbalance gas−spring without the gas−spring compression tool as
follows:
(1)
Make sure that the swivel lever (6) points inboard.
(2)
Close the passenger door (1) and latch.
(3)
Connect the cable (3) to the swivel lever (6) with the pin (7), the nylon washers (8),
the washer (9) and the cotter pin (10).
(4)
On the aft gas−spring make sure that the distance between the center of the pin
(15) and center of the bolt (32) to 41.02+00/−0.38 inches (104.19+00/−0.97 cm).
NOTE:
Make sure that each nylon washer (8) is installed in between the cable (3)
and the swivel lever (6).
(5)
If necessary, hold the cable terminal (5) and adjust the upper nut (2) to get the
correct cable length.  For more adjustment hold the cable terminals individually, and
adjust the related nuts (2).
NOTE:
Make sure that the cables are not twisted.
(6)
If necessary, adjust swivel lever (6) vertically with the adjustment bolt (12).
(7)
Loosen the nut (11) and turn the adjustment bolt (12) counter−clockwise to move
the swivel lever (6) to a lower position.  Turn the adjustment bolts (12) clockwise to
move the swivel lever (6) to a higher position.
(8)
Tighten the nut (11).
(9)
Adjust the passenger door counterbalance (Ref. TASK 52−11−17−820−802).
(10)
Adjust the passenger−door support−wheel system (Ref. TASK
52−11−13−820−802).
(11)
Do an operational test of the passenger−door support−wheel system (Ref. TASK
52−11−13−710−801).
(12)
Do an operational test of the passenger door counterbalance (Ref. TASK
52−11−17−710−802).
(13)
Lockwire the cable terminals (5).

K.
Install the spring rod assembly (1) between the lever assembly and the actuating lever
(9) as follows:
NOTE:
Make sure all the surfaces are clean with no corrosion, paint, grease, or other
contaminants.
(1)
Do a check of the spring rod assembly (1) length.
NOTE:
The nominal length of the spring rod assembly (1) is 11.93 in. (303.02
mm) between the rod end centers.
(2)
If necessary, adjust the length of the spring rod assembly (1) (Ref. TASK
52−11−15−830−801).

Install the spring rod assembly (1) to the lever assembly.
(4)
Wet install the bushing (8), the bolt (7), the washers (3), and the nut (5) with the
sealant 09−020 to connect the spring rod assembly (1) to the lever assembly.
NOTE:
Make sure the spring rod end is aligned in the center of the fork of the
actuating lever assembly.
(5)
Torque the nut (5) 10−12 lbf·in (1.13−1.36 N·m) and safety with the cotter pin (6)
(Ref. TASK 20−24−00−910−801).
(6)
Install the spring rod assembly (1) to the actuating lever (9).
(7)
Wet install the bushing (4), the bolt (2), the washers (3), and the nut (5) with the
sealant 09−020 to connect the push rod assembly (1) to the actuating lever (9).
NOTE:
Make sure the push rod end is aligned in the center of the fork of the
actuating lever.
(8)
Torque the nut (5) 10−12 lbf·in (1.13−1.36 N·m) and safety with the cotter pin (6)
(Ref. TASK 20−24−00−910−801).

52-42-00-820-803.title:
A.
Make sure of the conditions that follow:
(1)
Close and latch the avionics compartment door.
(2)
Measure the clearance between the door guide fittings and the frame guide fittings
as follows:
(a)
The clearance between the forward frame guide−fittings (left and right) and the
forward door guide−fittings (left and right) is between 0.020 ±.010 in. (0.51
±0.25 mm).
(b)
The clearance between the aft frame guide−fittings (left and right) and the aft
door guide−fittings (left and right) is between 0.020 ±0.010 in. (0.51 ±0.25
mm).
(c)
Add the left forward and aft guide fitting clearances and make sure that the
total clearance is between 0.040 ±0.020 in. (1.02 ±0.51 mm).
(d)
Add the right forward and aft guide fitting clearances and make sure that the
total clearance is between 0.040 ±0.020 in. (1.02 ±0.51 mm).
(e)
If necessary, adjust the clearance as follows:
1
Remove the necessary guide fitting.
2
Adjust the thickness of the laminated shim to get the correct clearance.
3
Install the guide fitting.
(3)
The clearance between the end of each roller and the track in which it moves is
between 0.035 ±0.015 in. (0.89 ±0.38 mm). Check the clearance at each 15 in.
(381 mm) of track. If necessary, adjust the clearance as follows:
(a)
Remove the rollers (Ref. TASK 52−42−00−820−803).
(b)
Add or subtract the shim washers to get the clearance.
1
Make sure that the total clearance for the forward rollers (left and right) is
between 0.070 ±0.030 in. (1.78 ±0.76 mm).
2
Make sure the total clearance for the aft rollers (left and right) is between
0.070 ±0.030 in. (1.78 ±0.76 mm).
(c)
Install the rollers (Ref. TASK 52−42−00−820−803)..
B.
Measure the clearance between the door stop−fitting screws and their frame stop fittings
are as follows:
(1)
Make sure clearance between the door stop−fitting screws (six locations) and their
frame stop fittings are 0.010±0.005 in. (0.25±0.13 mm).
(2)
If necessary, adjust the clearance as follows:
(a)
Loosen the lock nuts on the door stop−fitting screws.
(b)
Adjust the stop screws as necessary.

71-00-00-868-816.title:
TASK 71−00−00−868−816
Engine Emergency Procedures
1.
General
A.
The emergency procedures contained in this section identify the procedures that are
necessary to prevent the aircraft and crew from dangerous conditions that can occur.
When an emergency condition occurs the MASTER WARNING system, the EICAS
messages, or the applicable switch/lights of the system that has failed will come on.
B.
These procedures show the emergency conditions that could be found during engine
operation or engine start. These procedures show the necessary steps to identify the
failure and correct the conditions that follow to prevent damage to the engine or injury to
ground personnel.
C.
The emergency conditions are identified as follows in this procedure:
(1)
Internal Engine Fire (Post Shutdown refer to Table 512).
(2)
Internal Engine Fire (refer to Table 513).
(3)
External Engine Fire (refer to Table 514).

HIGH VIBRATIONS CAUSED BY THE FAN
Refer to Figure 106
A.
Definition of the Condition
(1)
In this condition, the EICAS display in the cockpit shows high fan vibrations during
engine operation. Possible causes for the high fan vibrations are:
(a)
An indication system problem (vibration pickup, vibration pickup harness or
signal conditioner).
(b)
An icing condition such as ice build−up on the fan.
(c)
One or more damaged fan blades.
(d)
One or more fan blades that are not free to move at the retaining pin
attachment point.
The most frequent cause for this is the build−up of retaining pin coating inside
the fan blade tang−holes. A migrated fan disk bushing, or the absence of
molykote on the edges of the fan blade tangs can also be causes.
(e)
An out−of−balance fan rotor
(f)
Mainline bearings.
(2)
The fan and the core vibration levels are sensed by a vibration pickup (EVM) that is
installed at the front frame/compressor casing splitline near the 2 o’clock position.
The fan vibration level is shown on the primary page of the EICAS display. The
display changes from green to amber if the fan vibration level is more than 2.7 mil.
(3)
Refer to AMM TASK 71−00−00−868−815 for the fan vibration limits.
B.
Troubleshooting
(1)
Before you start troubleshooting, find out the information that follows:
(a)
The following vibration symptoms can be an indication of a No. 5 bearing
retainer failure. An N1 vibration problem occurs suddenly, the engine had no
previous history of vibration problems and any combination of the following
conditions are observed:
1
How old is the engine? Is it relatively new in the 3000 hours TSN or TSSV
range?
2
Are there chips on the master chip detector or oil filter?
3
Did the N1 vibration problem occur suddenly?
4
During rapid acceleration does the N1 vibration jump up suddenly with no
vibration at low power setting? In some cases a "shudder" may be felt in
the aircraft. The indicated N1 vibration is in the 60−70 HZ range.
5
Unable to accomplish a fan trim balance despite multiple attempts and the
vibration levels are "jumping" around concurrent with the symptoms
mentioned above.

BLOCK NO.
TROUBLESHOOTING INSTRUCTIONS
2
The ENG SPEED switches on the ENGINE CONTROL panel in the flight
compartment must be set to ON for all usual conditions of operation. This lets
the N1 control system operate at high power settings. The only time that the
switches are set to OFF are during an N1 amplifier disable check, for
troubleshooting procedures, or during engine operation if the crew thinks there
is a N1 control system failure.
5
At the fuel control input shaft, the PLA must be set to 15°−18° with the throttle
set at idle.
6
With the compressor vanes in the full closed position, the rig marks on the
feedback−cable lever arm and on the fuel control must be aligned.
Refer to AMM TASK 75−31−03−000−801 to do a force gauge check to make
sure that the feedback cable moves freely. There must be no more than 10
pounds (44.5 N) force to move the cable, if it is disconnected at its upper end (at
the upper VG shaft attachment) and pulled. There must be no more than 1
pound (4.4 N) force to move the cable, if it is disconnected at its lower end (at
the fuel control lever arm) and pulled. If the force gauge check fails, find the
cause, and replace the cable if necessary.
14
If the mismatch is intermittent, the satisfactory N1 amplifier disable check results
will not necessarily mean that there is no N1 control system problem. It is
recommended that you examine the N1 control system components even if the
N1 disable check results are satisfactory (blocks 26 through 36).
32
To do the check:
Install the fan speed pick−up from the LH engine on the RH engine and the fan
speed pick−up from the RH engine on the LH engine.
33
To do the check:
Install the alternator stator from the LH engine on the RH engine and the
alternator stator from the RH engine on the LH engine.
34, 35
Repeat the amplifier disable check to find if the system has returned to normal.

LOW ENGINE PERFORMANCE

NOTE:
Use the procedure that follows if the engine performance shows an important
change, as given by the engine trend monitoring−system.
A.
Definition of the Condition
NOTE:
A variation in the ITT margin of 5° maximum as indicated by the trend
monitoring program is not unusual. During takeoff, one ITT point is recorded
for each flight by the MDC 10 seconds after weight−off−wheels. The ITT value
can change depending on the residual engine temperature (which has an
effect on the ITT overshoot properties), the power adjustment procedure or the
position of the ECS and the anti−ice bleed system.
(1)
Signs for a low engine performance are:
(a)
The failure to meet the power assurance limits.
(b)
A high ITT indication (an important change from the indications before).
(c)
A low ITT margin as indicated by the trend monitoring program.
(2)
Also refer to FIM 77−10−00, THERMOCOUPLE HARNESS.
B.
Troubleshooting
(1)
Before you start the troubleshooting, find out the information that follows:
(a)
Is the wind speed more than 20 knots.
(b)
Which maintenance procedure was done recently? For example: A water wash
of the compressor or other actions that may have disturbed the bleed air
system, or the removal of the fan rotor assembly from the engine.
(2)
Additional troubleshooting instructions:
(a)
Block No. 3:
Make sure that you hand−wash the fan blades, the EGVs and the inlet area
with a soft−bristled brush at the same time when you wash the compressor.
The cleanliness of the fan can have an important effect on a performance

27-00-10-000-802.title:
B.
The LRU STATUS page:
(1)
Look for fault messages for the LRU "CFMS". "NO FAULTS" means that all
monitored systems are normal and no messages exist. Check the LRU STATUS
page first when a problem is first suspected. If the STATUS condition shows
"FAILED" − replace the ECU (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−00−10−000−802).
(2)
If the STATUS condition shows OFF/NO OUTPUT TO DCU − make sure there is
power to the ECU as follows:
(a)
Make sure the circuit breaker K6 − CREW FORCE SYS on CBP−1 is closed.
(b)
With the circuit breaker closed and electrical power on, test for 28 volts dc at
the ECU mounting tray pin B15 and a ground at pin C15 of P14WR−B (Ref
WM 31−31−00)
(c)
If there is 28 volts dc at the pin, replace the ECU (Ref. AMM  TASK
27−00−10−000−802).
(d)
If there is not 28 volts dc at the pin, trace back through the wiring and repair
the wiring or replace the circuit breaker as necessary (Ref. WM 31−31−00).
C.
The LRU HISTORY page:
(1)
The LRU FAULT HISTORY page is useful to find a recurring problem. Look for fault
log messages for the LRU "CFMS". "NO FAULTS" means that no faults are stored
in the log.
D.
The LRU  DIAGNOSTIC DATA page:
(1)
Record the status of bits 22 through 14 (in binary mode) of CFMS label 350
diagnostic word. Remember that the bits show in descending sequence with bit 29
being the first digit on the left. Disregard bits 29 to 23. Refer to Table 101 for fault
designation and maintenance action.
E.
The excitation voltage from the ECU to the sensors is 5 volts ac. If the circuit breaker K6
− CREW FORCE SYS on CBP−1 is closed and CFMS label 350, bit 22 is set, test for 5
±0.3 volts ac at pins 7 and 8 on the sensor connectors before you replace a sensor. If
there is no power, test and repair the wiring as necessary. If the wiring is okay, replace
the ECU (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−00−10−000−802).
If there is an indication of a sensor failure, before replacing the sensor, disconnect the
electrical connector from the sensor and connect a known good one. Do the zero rigging
of the crew force measuring system (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−00−10−830−801). If the fault
clears, replace the applicable sensor. If the fault indication remains, check the wiring
from the connector to the ECU and repair the wiring as necessary. If the wiring is okay,
replace the ECU (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−00−10−000−802).
NOTE:
You can connect any known good spare sensor (rudder, elevator or aileron) at
each suspected sensor failure location, to check the condition on the installed
sensor. If you remove any sensor, you must  and do the zero rigging of the
crew force measuring system (Ref. AMM  TASK 27−00−10−830−801).

27-35-02-000-801.title:
WOW 1/ WOW 2 FAILURE
Weight−on−wheels discretes are supplied to the SPC from the PSEU.
For an "on ground" condition, the PSEU provides a ground to the
applicable WOW discrete from the SPC. This bit=1 when the SPC
detects a ground or open circuit failure in one or more or the discretes.
If the failure is internal to the PSEU, there will be PSS FAULT caution
messages on EICAS. If the are no PSS FAULT messages on EICAS,
the probable cause is a wiring fault between the SPC and PSEU, or a
failure of the SPC.
Do the steps that follow:
A.
If there are PSS FAULT EICAS messages refer to FIM 32−60−00.
B.
If there are no PSS faults, do the steps that follow:
(1) Replace the SPC with a known serviceable unit (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−35−02−000−801).
(2) If the fault occurs again, remove the SPC again and the
PSEU (Ref. AMM TASK 32−61−01−000−801).
(3) Test wiring for the WOW 1 and WOW 2 discretes between
the SPC and PSEU connector for shorts or open circuits (Ref.
WM 27−30−00). Repair the wiring as necessary.

27-53-00-780-801.title:
1
If a jam because of low temperature operation (water or too much grease
in the drive system) is suspected, do the steps that follows:
a
Disconnect the flexible drive shaft from each side of each applicable
actuator as necessary (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−801), the
drive shaft No. 2 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−802), the drive
shaft No. 3 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−803), the drive shaft No.
4 (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−804), the drive shaft No. 5 (Ref.
AMM TASK 27−53−10−000−805).
b
Examine the couplings for signs of water or corrosion. If water is found
in the flexible drive shafts, do the pressure test of the flexible drive
shaft (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−00−780−801). If the flexible drive shaft
passes the pressure test, clean the flexible drive shaft (Ref. AMM
TASK 27−53−10−220−802). Replace the flexible drive shafts that have
corrosion.
c
With the core disconnected at both ends, turn the core by hand to feel
for binding conditions, then remove the core.
d
Examine the core for too much grease (there should be a thin layer
only), damage to the core windings or corrosion.
e
Replace the flexible drive shafts that have damaged core windings or
corrosion.
f
If there is too much grease but no other damage, re−lubricate the core
with the correct quantity and type of grease (Ref. AMM TASK
12−20−27−640−806).
g
Install the core.  Make sure that the core moves in and out of the
casing freely and can be turned by hand.  Replace flexible drive shafts
that are difficult to turn by hand.
h
Remove the 4 actuators from the wing and do the low temperature
torque test on each one (Ref. AMM TASK 27−53−00−750−801).
Replace the actuators that fail the low temperature torque test.
2
If a jam because of mechanical drive system faults is suspected, do the
steps that follow:
a
Examine the flap actuators for visible signs of actuator damage or
leakage from the front housing of the actuator.  Replace actuators
where grease leakage is sufficient to form a run down the face of the
actuator front housing (gearbox).
b
Move the flap trailing edge up and down in line with each actuator as
the ballnut and forward end of the ball screw are observed.  If there is
visible fore/aft movement of the ballnut on the ballscrew, or of the
ballscrew in the actuator front housing, replace the actuator.  If you are
not sure about the amount of fore and aft movement and want to
measure the actuator’s endplay, refer to the Component Maintenance
Manual for the actuator.
c
Operate the flaps for 5 cycles, finishing with the flaps at 45 degrees.
During flap movement, listen to each actuator and also the PDU for
abnormal grinding, howling or other noises.  Replace a PDU or actuator
that makes abnormal sounds.

A.
Definition of a Hung Start
(1)
During an engine start, the N2 increase stops (N2 stagnation). Usually, if you try to
increase the engine speed with the throttle lever, it will have no effect. If the N2
indication stays the same for 5 seconds, stop the start and do the troubleshooting.

Before you try subsequent starts after a first hung start, dry motor the
engine (Ref. AMM TASK 72−00−00−868−811) to remove fuel from the
system.
B.

(1)
During a try to start the engine, the time to get to idle speed is longer than the limits
given in Figure 102.
